sections.title: Borrowing Wisely: Student Loans Explained
sections.summary: How federal student loans, Parent PLUS loans and private loans work, how to borrow only what you need, and what repaying looks like under the new federal rules.

blocks.heading: The short version
items: Use grants and scholarships first. Then, if you need to, borrow your own federal loans, and only what you need.
Parent PLUS is your parent's debt, and the bill doesn't drop if their income does. Talk it over as a family first.
Federal loan rules changed a lot in 2025 and 2026. Check StudentAid.gov or ask the college's financial aid office.
Payment too high? Call your loan servicer (the company that handles your loan bills) before you miss one.

blocks.heading: Federal loans for students
items: No credit check or credit history is needed. You sign and repay the loan yourself, even if you're under 18. If you die, the loan is canceled, so your family never has to pay it. It may also be canceled if you become totally and permanently disabled.

Direct Subsidized Loans are for undergraduates with financial need (the school's cost minus your Student Aid Index, a number the FAFSA works out from your family's finances). The government pays the interest (the extra cost of borrowing) while you're in school at least half-time and for six months after you leave.
Direct Unsubsidized Loans don't require financial need. Interest adds up the whole time, even while you're in school.
Dependent students (who report parent information on the FAFSA) can borrow $5,500 the first year, $6,500 the second and $7,500 a year after that, up to $31,000 in total.
Independent students can borrow $9,500 to $12,500 a year, up to $57,500 in total. You're independent if, for example, you're 24 or older, married, a veteran or supporting a child.

You can also count as independent if you were in foster care or a ward of the court any time after you turned 13, if a court set up a legal guardianship for you, or if you're homeless or at risk of it and not living with a parent or guardian. See Special situations on the FAFSA, and tell your counselor or the college's financial aid office.
You must be at least half-time (about half a full class load) in a degree or certificate program, at a college or trade school in the federal loan program. Less than full-time lowers your limit.

Cost: 6.52% fixed interest for loans first paid out July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. A 1.057% fee comes out before your school gets the money: on $5,500, about $5,442 reaches your school, but you owe $5,500. Rates for fall 2027 aren't set yet.

blocks.heading: Parent PLUS loans
items: A Parent PLUS loan is in your parent's name. Your parent must repay it, and it can't be moved to you later.

A biological or adoptive parent, or a stepparent on your FAFSA, can borrow. Grandparents and legal guardians can't unless they adopted you. If a grandparent or another relative is raising you, talk to the college's financial aid office.

Your parent applies after your FAFSA is done, usually at StudentAid.gov. Little or no credit history is fine. The check looks for serious problems, like a default or bankruptcy in the past five years.

If turned down, your parent can still borrow with an endorser (someone who agrees to repay if your parent doesn't) or by showing special reasons for the credit problems, and must also do credit counseling.

Limits: if you start college on or after July 1, 2026, all your parents together can borrow at most $20,000 a year and $65,000 in total for you. It can't be more than your cost of attendance minus other aid, your school may set a lower limit, and paying some back doesn't let your parents borrow more.
Cost: 9.07% fixed interest plus a 4.228% fee, for loans first paid out July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. Rates for fall 2027 aren't set yet.
If your parent asks, payments can wait while you're in school at least half-time and for six months after. Interest keeps adding up.
Have Parent PLUS loans for an older child? A new loan, or combining old loans (consolidating), can limit the old loans' payment plans too. Your parent should call their servicer first.

If your parent is turned down and doesn't get the loan another way, you may be able to borrow up to $4,000 more a year ($5,000 after your first two years) in unsubsidized loans. The financial aid office decides. Sometimes your parent doesn't have to apply first, for example if they're in prison, can't be found, have income only from public benefits or disability, or can't get federal aid because of immigration status. Reaching the PLUS limit, or a parent not wanting to borrow, doesn't count.

blocks.heading: Before your parent borrows
blocks.text: Parent PLUS can be easy to get and hard to pay back. No one checks whether the payments fit your family's budget. The payment is fixed: it doesn't go down if your parent's income drops or they retire, and Public Service Loan Forgiveness doesn't apply. If it goes unpaid, the government can take part of your parent's paycheck, tax refund and even Social Security. Example: $65,000 at 9.07% over 20 years is about $588 a month, or about $141,000 in total.

blocks.heading: Private loans
blocks.text: Private loans from banks, credit unions and others often need a credit history or a cosigner (someone who promises to pay if you don't). They usually cost more, rates may go up, and they lack federal benefits like income-based payments. Use them last, if at all. Be careful with high-cost career schools that push them or 'income share agreements', where you repay a share of future pay (see Paying for Career Training).

blocks.heading: Borrow only what you need
items: Fill out the FAFSA (the free federal aid form) every year. It's how you get federal loans.
In each aid offer, cover up the loans, including Parent PLUS, to see what each school really costs you.
Borrow only what's left after grants, scholarships and what your family can pay.
Ask the financial aid office about a tuition payment plan. Many schools let you pay monthly with no interest.
Loans aren't automatic. When you accept them, you can turn a loan down or take less. If you need more later, you can ask to increase it.

Before your first federal loan is paid out, finish entrance counseling (about 30 minutes online, in one sitting) and sign the loan contract (Master Promissory Note) at StudentAid.gov, using your own account. Your loan money can't be paid out until both are done, so don't wait. A parent taking Parent PLUS signs their own contract. No internet at home? Use a school or library computer, or ask the financial aid office for help.
Leftover loan money is still borrowed. Use it only for school costs, or give it back.

Changed your mind? You can usually cancel all or part of a loan within 14 or 30 days of the school's written notice that it was paid out. After that, you can still give it back within 120 days of when it was paid out, with no interest or fee. Ask the financial aid office how.

Need more than your own federal loans (up to $27,000 over four years if you're dependent)? Stop and look again. If your family's income dropped or you have big costs like medical bills, ask the financial aid office for a second look. Compare other schools' offers, and think about community college, an in-state public college or living at home. For a tax credit, see "Money back at tax time" in How paying for college or training works.

blocks.heading: What repayment looks like
items: Payments usually start six months after you graduate, leave school or drop below half-time. Talk to the financial aid office before you drop a class or withdraw. Dropping below half-time can start your six months, and withdrawing may mean you give back aid or owe the school money.
Tiered Standard Plan: the same payment each month for 10 to 25 years, depending on what you owe. Example: $27,000 at 6.52% is about $236 a month for 15 years, or about $42,400 in total.

Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP): your payment is based on your income and dependents, and can be as low as $10 a month. Pay on time and in full, and interest your payment doesn't cover is dropped. After 30 years of qualifying payments, the rest is forgiven (you may owe tax on it).

Public Service Loan Forgiveness: after 120 qualifying payments (about 10 years) while working full-time for a government or qualifying nonprofit employer, the rest is forgiven tax-free. For new loans, only RAP payments count. Which employers qualify can change.

blocks.heading: If your payment is too high
blocks.text: Call your loan servicer before you miss a payment, and ask about RAP. For loans made on or after July 1, 2027, you can't pause payments because you lost a job or are short on money, and general pauses for money problems are limited to 9 months in any 2-year period. Can't find your servicer? Log in at StudentAid.gov or call the Federal Student Aid Information Center at 1-800-433-3243. Never share your StudentAid.gov login, and never pay a company for help. Your servicer and StudentAid.gov help for free.

blocks.heading: If you fall behind
blocks.text: At 90 days late, your servicer tells the credit bureaus (companies that track how people pay bills). After 270 days without a payment, the loan is in default (officially unpaid). Then part of your paycheck, tax refund and even Social Security can be taken, and you can't get more federal student aid. Programs like loan rehabilitation can get a defaulted loan back on track, so call your servicer right away.

blocks.heading: If you or your parents are undocumented
items: U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens (like green card holders, refugees and asylees) can get federal loans, even if their parents are undocumented. The FAFSA doesn't ask about parents' status. Parents without a Social Security number can still make a StudentAid.gov account and fill out their part of the FAFSA.
Parents who aren't citizens or eligible noncitizens can't get Parent PLUS, but you may be able to borrow more (see Parent PLUS loans above).

Undocumented students, including DACA recipients, can't get federal loans but may qualify for state or college aid. Some states have their own form, like the CA Dream Act Application in California. Ask your counselor or the college's financial aid office which form to use.

This guide can't give legal advice. With immigration worries, read "Privacy and immigration" in Special situations on the FAFSA, and talk with a licensed immigration lawyer or a DOJ-accredited representative (a trained helper at a nonprofit approved by the U.S. Justice Department) before you apply. The USCIS "Legal services" page explains how to find them.

sections.title: Reading and Comparing Financial Aid Offers
sections.summary: How to read each aid offer, find your real net price, accept only what you need, and decide by your school's deadline (often May 1).

blocks.heading: The short version
items: Compare net prices: the full cost minus only grants and scholarships.
Take grants and scholarships first. Borrow last, and only what you need.
Finish verification early so your federal aid isn't held.
Offer too small, or your family's money changed? Ask each aid office to look again.
Most colleges ask you to decide by May 1. Check each school's date.

blocks.heading: What an aid offer is
blocks.text: An aid offer (or award letter) shows what a college or career/trade school can give or lend you for one school year. It comes after you're accepted, by email, by mail, or in the school's online portal. Set up each school's portal and school email right away, and check them every week for your offer and any requests for documents. No offer after a few weeks? Make sure the school is on your FAFSA form at StudentAid.gov (add it if it's missing), then call the aid office. Ask if they can go over the offer with your family by phone or video, in Spanish or another language. Your high school counselor can help, too.

blocks.heading: Sort the aid into piles
items: Gift aid: grants and scholarships, which you usually don't pay back. But if you stop going to all your classes early in a term, you may owe some federal grant money. Ask the aid office before dropping even one class.

Work-study: pay from a part-time job you usually find yourself. The offer shows the most you can earn, not a promised job. It isn't taken off your bill up front, so plan to use it for books and living costs.

Federal student loans: paid back with interest. Subsidized loans don't add interest while you're in school at least half time (about half a full class load); unsubsidized loans do. First-year students whose parents are on their FAFSA can usually borrow up to $5,500 a year, less if part time.
Other loans: Parent PLUS (your parent's federal loan), plus private, state, or school loans.

blocks.heading: Words you may see on an offer
items: Loans: any line that says loan, Direct, Stafford, PLUS, private, or institutional (from the school).
SAI (Student Aid Index): not your bill, just a number schools use to figure your aid.
Unmet need or gap: usually the part your family still has to cover.
In Spanish: "oferta de ayuda financiera" (aid offer), "beca" or "subvención" (grant), "préstamo" (loan).

blocks.heading: Find your net price
items: Use the same plan for every school: full or part time, and where you'll live. Part time means a smaller Pell Grant and smaller federal loans.
Start with the cost of attendance (COA), the school's full estimate for one year. It counts housing and food even if you live at home. Offer shows only your bill? Ask for the COA.
Subtract only grants and scholarships. What's left is your net price.
Multiply by the years in the program (for a short certificate, use the whole program). Ask how much costs may go up, and add up the loans for the whole program.
Ask if each grant comes back every year and what it takes to keep it, like certain grades, enough classes, and a new FAFSA each year.

blocks.heading: A loan is not a discount
blocks.text: Some offers count loans in "total aid" or subtract them from the cost, so a school looks cheaper than it is. Every loan, including Parent PLUS, has to be paid back with interest.

blocks.heading: Say yes only to what you need
items: Follow your offer's directions. Accept grants and scholarships first, then work-study if you'll work.

Borrow last, and only what you need. You can take all of a loan, ask for less, or say no. If you take less now, you can ask for more later. Some schools count a loan as accepted unless you turn it down.
Take your own federal loans first (subsidized, then unsubsidized), then Parent PLUS. Private loans, which usually have worse terms, come last.
First federal student loan? You get it only after entrance counseling (a short lesson on paying it back) and signing a Master Promissory Note (the loan contract).

Aid more than your bill? You get the extra, usually within 14 days. Many schools call this a refund, but loan money is still a loan. Any you don't need can be given back within 120 days with no interest or fees.

blocks.heading: Before your parent takes a Parent PLUS Loan
items: It's your parent's loan, and it can't be moved to you later. Being approved doesn't mean your family can afford it.
For students who start on or after July 1, 2026, all parents together can borrow at most $20,000 a year and $65,000 total per student.

Parent PLUS Loans made on or after July 1, 2026, have only fixed monthly payments, not a plan based on income. A new one can lock older Parent PLUS loans into fixed payments, too, so your parent should call the company that handles those loan bills first.
Parent turned down? Tell the aid office. You may be able to borrow more in your own federal loans. See "Borrowing Wisely: Student Loans Explained."

blocks.heading: If the offer isn't enough
items: Ask the aid office to take another look, and whether they'll consider a better offer from another school.
Ask about more grants, work-study, or a no-interest monthly payment plan.
Ask whether your state or college has a free-tuition program (see "State Aid and Promise Programs").
Keep applying for local scholarships. Never pay to apply or to get help with federal aid, and never share your StudentAid.gov username or password, even with someone helping you.
Starting at a community college and transferring later is a strong path. If a school costs more than your family can manage, picking another is a smart money choice, not a failure.

blocks.heading: If your family's money situation changed
blocks.text: The FAFSA uses tax information from a past year. If things changed, ask each school's aid office for a "special circumstances" review. Reasons can include:

items: A lost job, or less income or savings
Medical bills that insurance didn't cover
Child care costs, or a severe disability in your household
Losing your housing
A brother, sister, or parent also in college
Private school tuition for a younger brother or sister
A parent's death or a divorce (these are only examples, so ask)

blocks.text: Send a short letter with proof soon, or ask what else they accept. Approval isn't guaranteed and doesn't carry over to other schools, so ask every school.

blocks.heading: If you're selected for verification
blocks.text: Verification means proving your FAFSA information is correct. It doesn't mean you did anything wrong. If the Department of Education picks you, your FAFSA Submission Summary on StudentAid.gov shows an asterisk (*) next to your SAI. A school can also pick you, so watch for messages from every school. Each will tell you what to send, how, and by when. If a parent didn't file taxes, is paid in cash, has no Social Security number, or earned money in another country, ask the aid office what papers they'll accept. Don't send tax forms or Social Security numbers in a regular email.

blocks.heading: Finish verification early
blocks.text: Until verification is done, the school may hold your federal aid. If you never finish, you lose your Pell Grant for that year, must pay back any Pell or FSEOG (another federal grant) money you got, and can't get more federal loans (including Parent PLUS) or work-study. Finish even if you don't get a Pell Grant. Stuck getting a document? Tell the aid office right away.

blocks.heading: If you can't include your parents
blocks.text: Can't reach your parents, or contact with them would put you at risk? You may be able to get aid without their information. Say so on the FAFSA form, then contact each school's aid office. See "Special situations on the FAFSA."

blocks.heading: If you can't get federal aid
blocks.text: Undocumented students, including DACA recipients, can't get federal aid, so their offers may show only state aid, school aid, or private scholarships. Ask each school which form to fill out. If you're a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen, your parents' immigration status doesn't affect your federal aid. Worried about sharing information? See "Privacy and immigration" in "Special situations on the FAFSA" to find trusted legal advice.

blocks.heading: Career and trade programs
blocks.text: Some short programs can qualify for a Workforce Pell Grant (see "Pell Grants and Workforce Pell"). Before you borrow for a career school, make sure it takes federal aid. Check how many students finish and what they earn at https://collegescorecard.ed.gov. Be careful if a school pushes private or school loans.

blocks.heading: Outside scholarships
blocks.text: Tell the school you pick about every outside scholarship. It may lower other aid, so ask each school what it lowers first. The best answer is loans or work-study, not grants. New rule: if state, school, and private grants add up to your whole cost of attendance, you can't also get a Pell Grant.

blocks.heading: Deciding by May 1
items: Most colleges ask you to decide by May 1 if you applied regular decision or early action. Community colleges and career programs may differ, so check each school's date.
Say yes to only one school: send its forms and any deposit, then tell the others you won't attend.
Deposit hard to pay? Ask if the school can waive (drop) or delay it. Still waiting on an offer or verification near the deadline? Ask for more time.
Applied Early Decision and the aid isn't enough? Contact the school's admission and aid offices right away.

blocks.heading: After you say yes: your summer checklist
items: Check the school's portal and email every week and finish every to-do item, like sending your final high school transcript and any shot (immunization) records. Your aid can't be paid until verification and first-time loan steps are done.
Register for classes, and ask how many credits you need to keep each grant. Federal loans need at least half time.
Already have health insurance, like Medicaid? If the school charges every student for its plan, ask whether you can waive (skip) it, and by when.

Ask when your first bill is due and whether your aid will be paid by then. First-year students taking their first federal loan may wait 30 days into the term for it. Need books sooner? Ask the aid office.
Can't pay a bill? Before the due date, ask the aid office about a payment plan or emergency grants. Don't just skip enrolling.

sections.title: Paying for Career Training
sections.summary: Career training is a smart choice, not a backup plan: apprenticeships, grants, and job centers can help pay for it, and a few checks can protect you from programs that overpromise.

blocks.heading: The short version
items: Registered Apprenticeships pay you from day one. Find one at https://www.apprenticeship.gov/apprenticeship-job-finder.
File the free FAFSA as soon as you can at https://studentaid.gov.
Community college is often low cost. On average, grants cover tuition and fees for first-time, full-time students, but only if you apply.

Ask your counselor this week about free community college (“Promise”) programs. Some have applications due in the fall of senior year. For example, the class of 2027 must apply for Tennessee Promise by Nov. 2, 2026.
Before you sign up, get in writing whether your program can get a Pell Grant, and how much.

blocks.heading: Start now, in high school
items: Take career and technical education (CTE) classes, and ask about youth apprenticeships. In some, you start paid on-the-job learning at 16.

Finish high school or get a GED. You need one for most federal aid. Without one, ask a community college about “ability to benefit” career pathway programs, which let you get federal aid while you work toward a GED.

blocks.heading: Apprenticeships: get paid to learn
blocks.text: An apprenticeship is a real job that includes classes. A Registered Apprenticeship (approved by the U.S. Department of Labor or a state agency) pays you from day one.

items: The sponsor (the employer or group running the program) doesn't have to pay you for class time. Ask if it's paid, and if you'll owe anything for classes, books, or tools.
The federal minimum age is 16, but some programs require 18. Sponsors can add rules, like a diploma or GED, a math test, or a driver's license. Ask what each requires and when it takes applications.
Make sure it's a Registered Apprenticeship. Be careful if anyone asks you to pay a big fee to get an apprenticeship job.

blocks.heading: Costs besides tuition
blocks.text: Books, tools, uniforms, test fees, background checks, shots, and rides add up. Get a list of every cost before you enroll. Aid is usually paid in parts, so ask when it will arrive and whether the school can help with costs you pay first.

blocks.heading: Pell Grants
blocks.text: A Pell Grant (federal money you don't pay back) works at many community colleges and trade schools if the school takes part in federal aid and your program is long enough. For a regular Pell Grant, a certificate program usually needs at least 600 clock hours (class and lab hours), or 16 semester credits, and at least 15 weeks. Associate degrees qualify too. For 2026-27, the most is $7,395, for a full year of full-time study. Shorter programs and part-time students get less. Congress sets the 2027-28 amount.

blocks.heading: Workforce Pell for short programs
blocks.text: Starting July 1, 2026, Workforce Pell Grants can help pay for approved programs of 8 to just under 15 weeks (150 to 599 clock hours). Few programs may be approved yet, and students in them can't get federal loans. The average grant is expected to be about $1,710. Don't count on it until the school confirms in writing. See “Pell Grants and Workforce Pell.”

blocks.heading: How to apply for aid
items: Training starts before July 1, 2027? Use the 2026-27 FAFSA (Free Application for Federal Student Aid), open until June 30, 2027. Starting July 1, 2027, or later? Use the 2027-28 FAFSA, open since Sept. 23, 2026. Summer program? Ask the school which to use.

File as soon as you can, since some state grants are first come, first served. List every school you're thinking about (up to 20 online; you can change the list later). Not a senior yet? You'll usually file in the fall of senior year.
Free help: 1-800-433-3243 (English or Spanish), or 1-833-610-2590, then press 7 for other languages. For accounts, documents, and parent information, see “The FAFSA, Step by Step.”

blocks.heading: If you have to borrow
items: Try grants, apprenticeships, and job center help first. If you must borrow, use federal student loans (you apply with the FAFSA) before other loans.
When a school says you'll “get federal aid,” ask how much is grants and how much is loans. Some programs of 300 to 599 clock hours can get federal loans but not Pell Grants.

Be very careful with private loans, loans from the school, and payment plans that charge interest. A federal agency says an income share agreement (paying part of your future income for a set time) is credit, just like a loan.
A Parent PLUS loan is in your parent's name. Your parent must pay it back, even if you don't finish.
Before you sign, ask how much you'll owe in total and per month. Rule of thumb: don't borrow more in total than you expect to earn your first year on the job.

blocks.heading: American Job Centers
blocks.text: American Job Centers can help pay for training through a law called WIOA. This training money can help adults 18 and older, laid-off workers, and people ages 16 to 24 who are out of school and face barriers, like being homeless, in foster care, a parent, or having a disability. Students ages 14 to 21 from low-income families who face barriers may get tutoring, summer jobs, or paid work experience.

items: Job center training money works like a voucher (a credit you can only spend on training) for programs on your state's approved list. Ask the center for its list.
Centers use other grants first and may ask you to apply for a Pell Grant.
Centers may also help with transportation and child care. If the money pays for apprenticeship classes, it can also cover tools, books, and uniforms. Each area sets its own rules.
Almost all men ages 18 through 25 must register with Selective Service at https://www.sss.gov. You need to be registered to get job center help.
Find a center at https://www.careeronestop.org or call 1-877-US-2JOBS (1-877-872-5627). Centers must give you free language help, like an interpreter.

blocks.heading: More ways to pay
items: If you've been in foster care, ask your caseworker about an Education and Training Voucher (up to $5,000 a year) and whether your state waives tuition for foster youth.
Some employers pay for training. Ask when you apply for jobs.
Ask your counselor about scholarships for trade programs. Never pay to apply for one.
If you're at least half-time in training that leads to a recognized credential, your family may get money back at tax time through the American Opportunity Tax Credit. See “Money back at tax time.”

blocks.heading: Immigrant families
items: If you're a U.S. citizen or an eligible noncitizen, your parents' immigration status doesn't affect your federal aid, and the FAFSA doesn't ask about it. A parent without a Social Security number can still fill out their part.
Green card holders, refugees, asylees, and some other noncitizens can get federal aid. DACA recipients can't, but the FAFSA may help them get state or school aid.
Without a Social Security number, you can't fill out the FAFSA, but some states have their own aid form. Ask your counselor.

Worried about sharing information? Read “Privacy and immigration” in Special situations on the FAFSA, and talk with a licensed immigration lawyer or a DOJ-accredited representative (a trained helper approved by the Justice Department) before you decide.

Job centers can't treat you unfairly because of citizenship status if you're a citizen or an immigrant allowed to work in the U.S. Rules for immigrants in some education and job programs have been changing, so ask each program what it requires now.

blocks.heading: Programs that overpromise
blocks.text: Red flags: pressure to sign up today; a “guaranteed” job; pay or job promises they won't put in writing; pushing loan papers before you see your grants; asking for your StudentAid.gov username or password; or saying credits will transfer without showing which schools accept them. No papers to read before you commit? Don't enroll.

blocks.heading: Check a program before you sign
items: Look up the school at https://collegescorecard.ed.gov to see cost, graduation rate, what graduates earn and owe, and whether it's for-profit (run to make money for its owners).
Make sure it's accredited (checked by an approved group). Some fake schools make up their own accreditor, so check it at https://ope.ed.gov/dapip/. Federal aid works only at accredited schools.

If the job needs a state license, ask whether the program lets you take the test in your state, and what percent pass. If you have a criminal record, ask whether it could keep you from getting licensed before you pay anything.
Get in writing what percent of students finish and get jobs in the field, what recent graduates owe, and whether you can cancel and get your money back.

blocks.heading: If a school misled you
blocks.text: Report it at https://reportfraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general. If you used federal aid, also file a complaint at https://studentaid.gov/feedback-center/. If your school closed before you finished, or misled you, you may be able to get your federal student loans canceled. Call 1-800-4-FED-AID.
